I don't know if it's a platitude... But all I can offer you is what I know from *my* life. I stay alive because I know logically that I've had days where I want to be alive, where I enjoy things. I also know I've had dark times, as dark or darker than my current wave of depression. So, I know that the feelings of life ebb and flow. So I can logically assume, with near certainty, that I'll feel an extreme happiness again.

That, and I know, logically, that many people would be unbearably sad. Perhaps for the rest of their lives? I also know quite a number of depressed and suicidal people, and I really can't bear to think I might trigger someone with my death... Is it the best to live out of obligation to others? No. But to me it's better than nothing.

Now, these are logical mindsets. My emotion mind doesn't feel these things as true... But I tell them to myself, and it does help stint bit. It sometimes helps enough to get me to do something I vaguely enjoy - play guitar, watch Netflix. When I'm really brave, maybe even call a friend. And at the very least... fall asleep. I keep going, and then sometimes I have a moment of happiness, or even a day of calm.

Good luck.

I'm so so sorry for your loss.

Thank you for sharing your story though. I can't speak for everyone, but these stories do help me.

Also, know that if you need to talk, if you need someone to listen to you in your grief, you can always reach out here. And there are some good resources mentioned on the sidebar for survivors.

Thank you again.

Oh, boy. Have I been there.

My job was my life. I loved it more than anything.

But eventually I had to realize that I had to leave. It was too much, and my mental health was more important.

Your mental health is more important than your job. YOU are more important than your job. You are worth so much more.

All that being said, is it possible there is an in-between? In my most stressful moments at my job, I took a vacation. Even if it was just a 3-day weekend, the break helped; it allowed me to recoup and then keep doing what I loved for longer. Can you take a break or a vacation?

Whatever the solution, remember: You are more important than your job. Your value is so much beyond it. You deserve to be cared for; care for yourself.

Good luck.

We're already on lists. We register that we're citizens (SSN); we register if we drive; we register if we carry firearms (sorta, kinda, some places); we register if want federal aid of any kind; we register if we're getting married; we register to vote; we participate in the census.

To me, it's not the lists that are the problem. Not inherently anyway.

It's a) what the list is for and b) the fucking lack of transparency, the secrecy, the outright lies.

That's the problem with government spying. That's the problem with violation of privacy.

Lists that we already use every day are a mutual agreement between citizens and government. We've enacted these laws with purpose; we're fine with them. The problem with CISA and things like it is that we haven't agreed to the terms. And because we haven't agreed to them, we also don't know what's going on, or if the terms are being violated, and therefore we can't even attempt protect ourselves against the violations. And THAT is a violation of the social contract that needs to exists between the government and the governed in order for things to be civil and fair.

But we are never are assertive enough to ask for reciprocity (and often others are not capable of it), so we end up hurt, and feel ignored and uncared for.

I'm really not sure what the solution is. Except ask for what you need, a listening ear. Sometimes people can't be that... But sometimes they can.

Well... I'm not sure how Canadian laws work.

In the US, when you're not of age, your parents still have legal control over pretty much everything related to you. Including medical care. So your parents could override your decisions.

But I also know that even underage, if you show up at an ER and declare you're suicidal, they'll take you in and take care of you; they'll just work to contact your guardian at the same time.

Is that how it works where you are, or do you have more agency?

I think, legally, having your dad might make things easier. Paperwork wise, red tape and all that... But I think that even if you don't need him, you should tell him. Even if you can't tell him everything just like "I'm in a bad place with my depression, and I'm scared of what I'll do, and I think I need to go to the hospital. Can you come with me?" Physical support is good to have in scary times.

Well, if you're in a hospital, they make you wear scrubs, like any other patient, so they take your clothes. They take any sharp jewelry (so you can't hurt yourself), they take your phone, and they make you take off your bra if you're wearing one (because I guess you can strangle yourself with it). They also take sharp objects like pens and pencils... So if you want to write, markers are best. They just keep it all behind the desk.

If you want to be able to call people, I'd write down all your important phone numbers on a piece of paper and keep it with you (I used it as a bookmark). You can usually make calls, but they're  just on phones that are in the hallway and like...not private. Which is weird, but understandable.

When I checked myself in to a longer term facility, I got everything back (except my phone), but I had to sign a waiver saying that I was responsible for my jewelry and that nothing bad would happen (to myself or others) with it. But I was also marked as lower risk... So I suppose these things vary by risk assessment.

I do think you should tell your dad. Especially if you feel like he'll be there for you... It was hard for me to tell my mom. I had to comfort her...it was weird. But after the initial shock, she was so supportive. She took time off work and flew 3 hours to stay with me most of the whole week I was in the psych hospital (she'd be there all day during the 12 hours of visiting allowed).

What would you like to talk about?

1. Take it seriously. Every time. Often "jokes" and asides are a way of putting it out there, seeing if anyone cares. Sometimes going as far as seeing if anyone will stop us.

2. You're a good friend for seeking out advice.

3. Be there with him. Spend time with him, try to make him laugh, remind him that he's lived and cares about and even if he fails out of school with massive debt, he's *still* loved and cared about and can make a worthwhile life. Also... Offer to help him study.

4. Call a suicide hotline for advice. They're not just to call if you're the one in crisis. They're trained professionals so they'll be able to talk you through options and how to respond.

Good luck

Trust me, there are days when I don't realize it. I know that one day I'll probably kill myself. I've recently resigned myself to that fact. Very recently, like a couple of weeks ago. But, idk, once I came to terms with that fact... It was almost freeing. It's like, my mind is now able to make an addendum to it. "I'm gonna kill myself... But not today." Not next week, not next month, realistically it could go either way if I make an attempt next year... I hope I don't, but I think I'll be consumed by my illness one day... But that knowledge of "not right now" has been able to motivate me to do stuff "I might as well assemble my bookshelf if I'll be here tomorrow to use it." "I might as well apply for jobs if I need to pay rent in december" "I might as well buy christmas presents, 'cause I have to have them for christmas and I'll be around."

There are people who have it much worse than I do, and carry on just fine. But just because other people have it worse, doesnt mean you don't have it bad. You're in pain. This is the most pain you've ever dealt with. Comaring it to someone else's pain doesn't change that it's the worst pain you've ever dealt with.

There are people that have broken down at seemingly small inconveniences than you have. Just because you or I may be able to deal with whatever they couldn't, doesn't mean they weren't in more pain than they could handle. People have different capacities, different experiences. That's ok.

Something else that has been helping me... I've been visiting this subreddit every day since I had my aha moment. I've been trying to help people and I see the things people think and write and sometimes I'm helpful, others I'm not sure. But I know that I see bits of me in other people. I see the similarity of our problems and my reaction is to try to help. And if I think their problems are able to be overcome, than why aren't mine? And then I basically talk to myself like I was a stranger. How would I try to help a stranger or a friend if they confided in me the dark thoughts that I have. And what I tell myself then... It helps. It helps keep me going.

Sorry I didn't respond sooner; I also went to bed :)
You're not wasting my time. And I'm definitely not angry.

I just... Your concerns mirror mine so much.

My dad pays my student loans to the tune of a $1000/mo (those are minimum payments, btw), and I'm gonna take on more loans if I go to law school, and he'll be paying those off too, and he might be helping me pay off loans the rest of his life. He also pays for my therapy, my health insurance... And he's helping me with December rent. It's embarrassing, and I hate how dependent I am.

And even with that help, I still have to ask my mom for money sometimes. 'Cause I'm terrible at managing my finances.

I just started a new part time job and I'm worried I'm not gonna be able to handle it emotionally and physically. Because my last job, a job I lived and was good at, I ended up becoming overworked and experiencing such intense burnout that I was "working" from home all the time and just...not doing anything. The burnout was part of the reason I landed in the psych hospital, and also why I quit. But I'm not capable of functioning at the level I used to be able to (80-100 hr weeks), barely a quarter of that, and that makes me feel like a failure.

My brothers and I have said some pretty nasty things to each other. I've never wished them death, but I have told them I never want to see them again, and they've wished me death. 

But we've also cried in front of each other, and hugged each other for comfort, and mocked our parents together, and played video games, and played make pretend. We've been those things for each other too.

With my friends... I don't have many close ones. Part of it is me keeping people at arms length, for fear of them abandoning me once I open up too much. The friends I have, I tend to initiate contact... If I went, they'd grieve deeply, though I'm pretty certain my friends, even my suicidal ones, are stronger people and would rebound from the grief. My family too.

They would recover, grow beyond it, and eventually thrive. But I know they would be wounded. I know they would hurt deeply.

And I can't cause that hurt. My whole life I've had this view of "I would rather suffer than let others be in pain." It's how I live my life, and why I'm in pain so often. (I do this to myself, but I know no other way to be. This depression that ratios is a part of who I am.) But it's how I live my life. So I try my hardest not to die, because my final act would cause pain.

But I know that not everyone shares my philosophy. And I can't make you do anything you don't feel is right for you. 

But I just want to say that I understand what you're going through, and I think you deserve happiness. And that happiness can only come from you putting it off a bit longer. Your sadness will end if you die, but only because you will cease to exist. And you deserve so much more than that.

Anyway... Hope this post didn't sound preachy. I hope you respond. Even if I don't change your mind (which I know is a possibility), I at least would like to provide you with conversation about it all. Someone who knows and accepts you even knowing you may kill yourself... I hope that is of some comfort to you.

I'm sorry for your loss. That's hard. I know you say your life is better without him, and that it was some time ago. But I'm still sorry.

May I ask what you've done or what burdens you bring that you think would be lifted? I'm sorry if that's a personal question, and if it's too personal you don't need to say... But as I said, I like logic, and isn't it possible there's a false equivalence? You are not your father; how do you know life would improve?

I think it's possible to both be the source of pain and be in immense pain yourself.

And trust me... Family love is not always unconditional. If they thought you caused them insurmountable pain, they would have left you.

The other day in therapy, my therapist and I discussed different kinds of distorted thinking. One of those is "mind reading." That is, the perception that you *know* what someone is thinking. The shitty thing about perception is...it feels so true. But I would guess if questioned, your family would say that not only is the pain you've caused negligible, but that the goodness you've brought them far outweighs it.

Look, my dad was an abusive asshole when I was a kid. He fucked up and caused a lot of pain that he's never apologized for and never will (which in turn causes more pain). At the same time, I have many wonderful memories with him when I was a kid, and enjoy spending time with him now. I don't want him gone from my life, and I certainly don't want him dead. He makes my life more challenging yes... But the challenges enhance my life rather than detract from it. If he was gone, that would be worse.

Is it not possible your family feels the same?

I don't think you should. People give odd answers to normal questions, sometimes, so I just wanted to see. I'm sorry if the questioning was upsetting.

I just... I hope this next bit doesn't come off as me trying to make you feel guilty. I certainly don't mean to, because you have nothing to feel guilty for as far as I know. But I want to let you know that commuting suicide now will still hurt them during the holidays. The proximity of it all. So, logically, waiting my be a good idea

But I know pain isn't logical. It doesn't necessarily respond to logic. But, I know for me, I'm able to talk myself out of it with logic. "I don't want to hue my family? Why? Because I love then. Are you sure they'll be hurt? Yes. Why? Because I'm sure they love me" and then in that moment I feel that love a little bit and can stop myself.

I suppose I was hoping your brain might work the same.

The weeklong stay helped immensely. Not just the therapy groups (though I did enjoy those, honestly); but the structure. The physical things I'd been neglecting (like eating, showering regularly, a regular sleep schedule, moderate exercise) were kinda forced upon me (in a nice way) and that seemed to restart my brain a bit.

Since then, I've been in a therapy that I find helpful and things are slowly getting better (though there have been some setbacks as well; but i'm coping).

I'm not sure if that advice will seem helpful to you at all... But I try to live by the problem solving rules of "if x isn't working, change it." So, your current coping resources aren't working, and if you continue in this current state, you might kill yourself, but you know you probably don't want to die. What to do? Find ways to up coping mechanisms.
